items.q: A 64-year-old man undergoes diagnostic femoral angiography through a 5F sheath. The sheath is removed with normal clotting and no heparin on board. The registrar asks the intern how long to hold manual pressure and what position the patient keeps afterwards. Which combination follows standard groin care?
o: Five minutes pressure then sit upright at once
Fifteen to twenty minutes pressure then lie flat with the leg straight
One minute pressure then walk to the ward
No pressure needed when the sheath is small
items.exp:
**Answer: B - Fifteen to twenty minutes pressure then lying flat with the leg straight.** Manual compression holds the femoral puncture closed while lying flat keeps the groin straight and watched.
**Why the others are wrong**
- A: Five minutes rarely seals an arterial hole and sitting bends the groin
- C: One minute cannot achieve haemostasis and walking invites bleeding
- D: No pressure at all guarantees haematoma
**Key point:** Manual pressure with flat bed rest.
r: Incorrect. Five minutes rarely seals arterial holes.
Correct. Pressure with flat rest seals groins.
Incorrect. One minute cannot stop bleeding.
items.kp: Manual compression with flat bed rest seals femoral punctures.

items.q: A 58-year-old woman has a large-bore femoral sheath after uterine artery embolisation. The operator deploys a suture-mediated closure device and the groin looks dry. The ward nurse asks when she may first walk compared with manual compression. Which statement about suture closure is correct?
o: She walks sooner than after manual compression in selected patients
She must never walk again after any closure device
The stitch dissolves the artery wall completely
Suture devices work only in veins
items.exp:
**Answer: A - Earlier walking than after manual compression in selected patients.** Suture-mediated closure stitches the arterial wall for large sheaths and allows earlier ambulation in suitable patients.
**Why the others are wrong**
- B: Never walking again defeats the purpose of closure devices
- C: The stitch closes the hole rather than dissolving the wall
- D: Suture devices are designed for arterial punctures
**Key point:** Suture closure allows earlier walking.
r: Correct. Suture closure permits earlier walking.
Incorrect. Stitches close rather than dissolve.
items.kp: Suture-mediated closure allows earlier ambulation after large sheaths.

items.q: A 71-year-old man on the cath-lab table receives full heparin during a prolonged mesenteric intervention through a femoral sheath. At the end the groin oozes briskly despite pressure. The anaesthetist suggests protamine for every heparinised case as routine. Which approach to heparin reversal follows CIRSE peri-procedural guidance?
o: Reserve protamine for bleeding punctures rather than routine reversal
Reverse every heparinised case regardless of bleeding
Give protamine before the procedure starts
Never remove the sheath once heparin is given
items.exp:
**Answer: A - Protamine reserved for bleeding punctures rather than routine reversal.** Routine reversal invites thrombosis so protamine is kept for punctures that bleed despite pressure.
**Why the others are wrong**
- B: Routine reversal trades bleeding for clot risk
- C: Pre-procedure protamine would defeat heparin protection
- D: Sheaths must come out once clotting recovers
**Key point:** Protamine only for bleeding heparinised punctures.
r: Correct. Reserve protamine for bleeding holes.
Incorrect. Sheaths come out when safe.
items.kp: Protamine reverses heparin only when the puncture bleeds.

items.q: A 45-year-old woman returns to the ward after femoral angiography. The nurse finds the right foot pale with no palpable dorsalis pedis while the left foot pulses normally. The groin looks flat with no swelling. Which complication does the lost pulse with a flat groin suggest?
o: Arterial thrombosis or dissection of the access vessel
Simple vasovagal faint needing fluids only
Contrast allergy causing pale skin
Successful closure with expected pulse loss
items.exp:
**Answer: A - Arterial thrombosis or dissection of the access vessel.** A lost distal pulse with a flat groin points inside the artery to clot or an intimal flap, not to external bleeding.
**Why the others are wrong**
- B: Faints recover pulses rather than losing one foot pulse
- C: Allergy causes hives and wheeze rather than single-limb pallor
- D: Successful closure preserves distal pulses
**Key point:** Lost pulse means thrombosis or dissection.
r: Correct. Lost pulses mean clot or flap.
items.kp: A lost distal pulse after access means thrombosis or dissection.

items.q: A 62-year-old man notices a painful pulsing lump in his right groin nine days after femoral catheterisation. Duplex shows a 3 cm pseudoaneurysm with a narrow neck and swirling flow. He takes aspirin with normal clotting otherwise. Which treatment best suits this symptomatic femoral pseudoaneurysm?
o: Ultrasound-guided thrombin injection into the sac
Antibiotics alone for six weeks
Chest physiotherapy and reassurance
Immediate major bypass surgery in every case
items.exp:
**Answer: A - Ultrasound-guided thrombin injection into the sac.** Thrombin injected under ultrasound clots the sac while the narrow neck protects the artery, suiting symptomatic pseudoaneurysms.
**Why the others are wrong**
- B: Antibiotics treat infection rather than flowing sacs
- C: Physiotherapy cannot clot a pseudoaneurysm
- D: Bypass is reserved for failed or infected cases
**Key point:** Thrombin injection for femoral pseudoaneurysm.
r: Incorrect. Bypass is a last resort.
items.kp: Symptomatic pseudoaneurysm needs ultrasound-guided thrombin.

items.q: A 69-year-old woman has a 6F femoral sheath removed after mesenteric stenting. The operator places a collagen plug device and the track seals at once. The junior doctor asks where the plug sits and why infection risk stays low. Which description of collagen plug closure is correct?
o: The plug seals the tissue track outside the artery, leaving nothing inside the lumen
The plug floats freely inside the aorta
The plug replaces the need for any groin watching
Plugs are placed inside the heart chambers
items.exp:
**Answer: A - The plug seals the tissue track outside the artery, leaving nothing inside the lumen.** Collagen plugs close the track from outside the vessel wall so no foreign body sits in flowing blood.
**Why the others are wrong**
- B: Free-floating plugs would embolise downstream at once
- C: Every groin still needs watching after any device
- D: Cardiac chambers are never involved in groin closure
**Key point:** Collagen plugs seal outside the artery.
r: Correct. Plugs seal the track externally.
items.kp: Collagen plugs seal the track outside the arterial lumen.

items.q: A 74-year-old man with a heavily calcified femoral artery needs large-bore access for complex embolisation. The operator chooses a clip-based closure device rather than suture. The trainee asks why calcium changes the choice. Which reason best supports clip closure in calcified walls?
o: Needles cross calcified walls poorly so clips that cap the hole suit better
Calcium makes arteries vanish on ultrasound
Clips dissolve calcium deposits permanently
Calcified arteries never bleed after puncture
items.exp:
**Answer: A - Needles cross calcified walls poorly so capping clips suit better.** Suture needles struggle through calcium while clip devices cap the puncture from outside, suiting diseased walls.
**Why the others are wrong**
- B: Calcified arteries still show on ultrasound
- C: Clips close holes rather than dissolving calcium
- D: Calcified vessels bleed like any other
**Key point:** Clips suit calcified arterial walls.
r: Incorrect. Clips close rather than dissolve.
items.kp: Clip devices suit heavily calcified access walls.

items.q: A 55-year-old man has a closure device deployed after femoral angioplasty, but brisk bleeding continues through the device with groin swelling. Pressure with gauze has not yet been tried. Which immediate fallback does device failure demand?
o: Direct manual compression over the puncture at once
Immediate leg amputation
Discharge home while bleeding continues
Start thrombolysis through the bleeding hole
items.exp:
**Answer: A - Direct manual compression over the puncture at once.** Every closure device can fail, and firm hand pressure over the hole remains the universal rescue.
**Why the others are wrong**
- B: Amputation is never indicated for groin bleeding
- C: Discharging a bleeding groin invites catastrophe
- D: Thrombolysis worsens active bleeding
**Key point:** Device failure falls back to manual pressure.
r: Incorrect. Bleeding groins stay in hospital.
items.kp: Failed closure devices demand immediate manual compression.

items.q: A 61-year-old woman takes daily aspirin after a coronary stent and now needs diagnostic femoral angiography for gut bleeding. The cardiologist advises on tablets through the procedure. Which peri-procedural antiplatelet plan follows standard IR practice for diagnostic work?
o: Continue aspirin through diagnostic angiography
Stop all tablets for a month beforehand
Double every dose on the morning of the case
Switch aspirin to an intramuscular injection
items.exp:
**Answer: A - Continue aspirin through diagnostic angiography.** Diagnostic punctures seal safely with aspirin on board, and stopping risks stent thrombosis for no groin benefit.
**Why the others are wrong**
- B: Month-long stops invite stent clots
- C: Doubling doses raises bleeding without benefit
- D: No intramuscular aspirin exists for this purpose
**Key point:** Aspirin continues through diagnostic access.
items.kp: Diagnostic angiography proceeds with aspirin continued.

items.q: A 68-year-old man on warfarin with a mechanical mitral valve needs elective uterine fibroid embolisation planning via femoral access. His thrombotic risk is very high and his INR is therapeutic. Which bridging decision best balances clot against groin bleeding?
o: Bridge warfarin only when thrombotic risk outweighs groin bleeding
Stop warfarin forever without any plan
Continue full warfarin through large-bore puncture
Refuse all procedures in valve patients
items.exp:
**Answer: A - Bridge only when thrombotic risk outweighs groin bleeding.** High valve-clot risk justifies bridging while low-risk cases simply pause warfarin, balancing both dangers.
**Why the others are wrong**
- B: Forever stopping invites valve thrombosis
- C: Full anticoagulation through large holes bleeds
- D: Valve patients undergo IR with planning
**Key point:** Bridging follows thrombotic versus bleeding balance.
items.kp: Warfarin bridging follows clot-versus-bleed balance.

items.q: A 59-year-old man returns from femoral angioplasty with a tense painful groin swelling and a falling blood pressure two hours later. His haemoglobin drops by 3 g/dL and his flank looks bruised. The femoral pulse feels full above a silent swelling. Which bleeding site does this falling haemoglobin with flank bruising suggest?
o: Retroperitoneal bleeding from a high puncture above the ligament
Simple skin bruise needing no action
Contrast allergy with delayed swelling
Successful haemostasis with expected swelling
items.exp:
**Answer: A - Retroperitoneal bleeding from a high puncture above the ligament.** High sticks bleed behind the peritoneum where pressure cannot reach, showing flank bruising with falling haemoglobin and shock.
**Why the others are wrong**
- B: Skin bruises never drop pressure or haemoglobin
- C: Allergy causes hives rather than flank blood
- D: Successful closure keeps vitals stable
**Key point:** Flank bruise with shock means retroperitoneal bleed.
items.kp: Flank bruising with shock after access means retroperitoneal bleeding.

items.q: A 52-year-old woman has heparinised femoral access for a long visceral embolisation. Before pulling the sheath the operator requests a bedside clotting test. The nurse asks which test guides sheath removal timing after heparin. Which bedside test best times sheath pulling?
o: Activated clotting time checked at the bedside
Urine pregnancy test at the bedside
Bedside blood glucose reading
Room temperature on the wall thermometer
items.exp:
**Answer: A - Activated clotting time checked at the bedside.** The activated clotting time tracks heparin effect and tells the operator when clotting has recovered enough to pull safely.
**Why the others are wrong**
- B: Pregnancy tests never guide sheath timing
- C: Glucose readings ignore heparin effect
- D: Room temperature cannot measure clotting
**Key point:** Bedside clotting time guides sheath removal.
items.kp: Sheath removal waits for bedside clotting recovery.

items.q: A 66-year-old man develops a continuous machinery bruit over his femoral puncture site with a palpable thrill one week after catheterisation. Duplex shows arterial flow directly into the adjacent vein throughout the cardiac cycle. Which access complication does continuous bruit with thrill define?
o: Arteriovenous fistula between artery and vein
Simple haematoma resolving normally
Deep vein thrombosis of the calf
Cellulitis of the groin skin
items.exp:
**Answer: A - Arteriovenous fistula between artery and vein.** A needle track joining artery to vein shunts flow continuously, giving machinery bruit with thrill on duplex.
**Why the others are wrong**
- B: Haematomas lack continuous bruits or thrills
- C: Calf clots cause swelling rather than bruits
- D: Cellulitis causes redness rather than thrills
**Key point:** Continuous bruit means arteriovenous fistula.
r: Correct. Bruit with thrill means fistula.
Incorrect. Clots swell rather than bruit.
Incorrect. Cellulitis reddens rather than thrills.
items.kp: Continuous machinery bruit after puncture means arteriovenous fistula.

items.q: A 49-year-old woman needs repeat hepatic chemoembolisation three days after a right femoral puncture. Both groins look clean with no bruising. The operator plans the second access route. Which side best suits re-puncture within days of the first stick?
o: The opposite left groin to let the first hole heal
The exact same hole while it still bleeds
The neck vessels without any reason
No access ever again after one puncture
items.exp:
**Answer: A - The opposite left groin to let the first hole heal.** Fresh puncture tracks seal poorly when re-entered within days, so the opposite groin protects the healing hole.
**Why the others are wrong**
- B: Re-entering a fresh hole disrupts its seal
- C: Neck sticks add stroke risk without benefit
- D: Repeat procedures routinely need fresh access
**Key point:** Early re-puncture uses the opposite groin.
items.kp: Re-puncture within days favours the opposite groin.

items.q: A 63-year-old man goes home six hours after diagnostic femoral angiography with a dry groin and stable observations. The nurse gives discharge warnings before he leaves. Which safety-net advice best suits same-day discharge after femoral access?
o: Return at once for spreading bruise, numbness, pallor or severe pain
Ignore all groin changes for a month
Remove the dressing and soak in a hot bath tonight
Run five kilometres to test the groin tonight
items.exp:
**Answer: A - Return at once for spreading bruise, numbness, pallor or severe pain.** Delayed bleeding, thrombosis and pseudoaneurysm declare themselves through bruise spread, numbness, pallor and pain.
**Why the others are wrong**
- B: Ignoring changes misses salvageable complications
- C: Hot soaks soften fresh clots and restart bleeding
- D: Running stresses fresh seals dangerously
**Key point:** Discharge warnings target bruise, numbness and pallor.
r: Correct. Red flags mean return at once.
items.kp: Discharge advice warns of bruise, numbness, pallor and pain.

items.q: A 57-year-old man has a femoral sheath removed while fully heparinised because the lab must close urgently. The groin bleeds briskly despite twenty minutes of pressure. Bloods show a very prolonged clotting time. Which immediate step best controls this heparinised bleeding puncture?
o: Sustained pressure with protamine reversal for the bleeding hole
Heparin infusion to keep the hole open
Walking the patient to compress by movement
Aspirin loading to seal the puncture
items.exp:
**Answer: A - Sustained pressure with protamine reversal for the bleeding hole.** Active bleeding through heparin effect needs both mechanical pressure and reversal of the anticoagulant driving it.
**Why the others are wrong**
- B: More heparin worsens the bleeding directly
- C: Walking disrupts pressure and restarts bleeding
- D: Aspirin adds platelet blockade to heparin harm
**Key point:** Bleeding heparinised holes need pressure plus protamine.
r: Correct. Pressure with reversal controls bleeding.
items.kp: Heparinised bleeding punctures need pressure with protamine reversal.

items.q: A 70-year-old woman with a small 4F diagnostic sheath asks why she must still lie flat for hours when the hole looks tiny. The nurse explains what bed rest prevents after any arterial stick. Which purpose of flat bed rest after small sheaths is correct?
o: Keeping the groin straight and still while the seal firms up
Treating the underlying arterial disease
Dissolving the femoral artery completely
Preventing all future heart attacks
items.exp:
**Answer: A - Keeping the groin straight and still while the seal firms up.** Hip flexion tugs fresh seals open, so flat rest with a straight leg protects even small holes until firm.
**Why the others are wrong**
- B: Bed rest never treats arterial disease
- C: Dissolving arteries would be catastrophic
- D: Heart attacks need drugs rather than bed rest
**Key point:** Bed rest protects fresh seals from hip flexion.
items.kp: Flat bed rest keeps fresh arterial seals undisturbed.

items.q: A 60-year-old man develops fever with spreading groin redness and pus five days after a collagen plug closure. Blood cultures grow skin flora and the track looks infected. Which closure-related infection principle guides this infected plug track?
o: Infected foreign bodies in the track need removal with antibiotics
Plugs sterilise themselves within days
Fever after closure always means malaria
Infected tracks heal faster when left closed
items.exp:
**Answer: A - Infected foreign bodies in the track need removal with antibiotics.** Bacteria coat foreign material where drugs alone cannot clear them, so infected plugs come out with antibiotic cover.
**Why the others are wrong**
- B: Plugs never self-sterilise once infected
- C: Malaria causes cyclical fever rather than groin pus
- D: Closed infected tracks form abscesses
**Key point:** Infected plug tracks need removal plus antibiotics.
items.kp: Infected closure tracks need plug removal with antibiotics.

items.q: A 54-year-old woman reports numbness over her front thigh after a prolonged femoral procedure with heavy pressure. Examination shows reduced sensation in the femoral nerve distribution with weak knee extension. Which pressure-related nerve injury does this anterior thigh numbness suggest?
o: Femoral nerve compression from haematoma or heavy pressure
Stroke causing isolated thigh numbness
Contrast allergy affecting one nerve
Successful anaesthesia lasting forever
items.exp:
**Answer: A - Femoral nerve compression from haematoma or heavy pressure.** The femoral nerve runs beside the artery where haematomas and hard pressure bars squeeze it, dulling the front thigh.
**Why the others are wrong**
- B: Strokes cause broader deficits rather than groin patterns
- C: Allergy never singles out one nerve
- D: Prolonged numbness needs urgent review
**Key point:** Thigh numbness means femoral nerve compression.
items.kp: Anterior thigh numbness after access means femoral nerve compression.

items.q: A 67-year-old man has brisk groin bleeding that continues despite thirty minutes of correct manual pressure and protamine. Duplex shows a large arterial wall defect with active extravasation. Which escalation best suits pressure-resistant arterial bleeding with a large defect?
o: Surgical repair or covered stent of the damaged artery
Longer waiting without any escalation
Thrombolysis into the bleeding defect
Compression of the opposite groin instead
items.exp:
**Answer: A - Surgical repair or covered stent of the damaged artery.** Large wall defects that defeat pressure and reversal need mechanical closure by surgeons or a covered stent.
**Why the others are wrong**
- B: Waiting lets shock deepen unchecked
- C: Thrombolysis dissolves the very clot needed
- D: The opposite groin cannot stop this bleeding
**Key point:** Pressure-resistant defects need surgery or covered stents.
items.kp: Pressure-resistant arterial defects need surgical or stent repair.

items.q: A 50-year-old woman undergoes femoral venous sampling with a small sheath and asks whether closure devices are needed as for arterial cases. The operator explains how venous holes differ from arterial holes. Which statement about venous puncture closure is correct?
o: Low-pressure venous holes usually seal with brief pressure alone
Venous holes need suture devices in every case
Veins bleed harder than arteries always
Venous punctures never need any watching
items.exp:
**Answer: A - Low-pressure venous holes usually seal with brief pressure alone.** Veins run at low pressure so small holes close with short compression, unlike high-pressure arterial sticks.
**Why the others are wrong**
- B: Routine devices over-treat simple venous holes
- C: Arteries out-bleed veins at pressure
- D: Every puncture still needs watching
**Key point:** Venous holes seal with brief pressure.
r: Correct. Veins seal with brief pressure.
items.kp: Small venous holes close with brief manual pressure.

items.q: A 72-year-old man with severe obesity needs femoral access and the operator marks landmarks carefully before draping. The trainee asks why body habitus raises access risk. Which obesity-related access principle is correct?
o: Deep vessels with shifting landmarks raise malposition and bleeding risk
Obesity makes arteries disappear permanently
Heavy patients never bleed from punctures
Landmarks stay identical regardless of habitus
items.exp:
**Answer: A - Deep vessels with shifting landmarks raise malposition and bleeding risk.** Thick tissue hides pulses and lets needles wander high or low, so ultrasound guidance matters most in obesity.
**Why the others are wrong**
- B: Arteries persist but hide beneath tissue
- C: Obesity raises rather than removes bleeding
- D: Landmarks shift badly with habitus
**Key point:** Obesity raises malposition and bleeding risk.
r: Correct. Deep vessels wander off landmarks.
items.kp: Obese access needs ultrasound as landmarks shift.

items.q: A 47-year-old man has his femoral sheath pulled and holds pressure himself while chatting, releasing every minute to check. Bleeding restarts repeatedly over half an hour. The nurse takes over with uninterrupted pressure. Which compression discipline stops this cycle of re-bleeding?
o: Continuous uninterrupted pressure without peeking until time elapses
Repeated peeking to check progress faster
Pressure applied beside the hole rather than over it
Blowing on the groin to dry the blood
items.exp:
**Answer: A - Continuous uninterrupted pressure without peeking until time elapses.** Each early release tears the forming clot, so unbroken pressure over the hole lets the seal build once.
**Why the others are wrong**
- B: Peeking tears each forming clot
- C: Beside-the-hole pressure misses the leak
- D: Blowing dries skin rather than sealing arteries
**Key point:** Unbroken pressure without peeking seals groins.
r: Incorrect. Pressure must sit over holes.
items.kp: Manual compression must stay continuous without peeking.

items.q: A 65-year-old woman on dual antiplatelets after a recent drug-eluting coronary stent needs urgent large-bore femoral embolisation for bleeding. Cardiology advises continuing both tablets through the case. Which closure plan best suits large sheaths with continued dual antiplatelets?
o: Suture-mediated closure with prolonged watching for oozing
No closure method works with any tablet on board
Rubber band around the thigh as a tourniquet
Stopping both tablets against cardiology advice
items.exp:
**Answer: A - Suture-mediated closure with prolonged watching for oozing.** Stitch closure gives large holes their best seal while extended observation catches the oozing that tablets prolong.
**Why the others are wrong**
- B: Suture closure seals through platelet blockade
- C: Tourniquets threaten the whole limb
- D: Overriding cardiology risks stent thrombosis
**Key point:** Large sheaths on tablets need suture closure plus watching.
items.kp: Large-bore access on dual tablets needs suture closure with long watching.

items.q: A 56-year-old man has a dry groin after suture closure and walks to the bathroom two hours later against advice, then notices fresh bleeding soaking the dressing. Pressure restarts and the bleeding stops. Which ambulation principle does this early-bleed episode teach?
o: Walk only when the local protocol time has elapsed with a dry groin
Walking immediately tests closure strength safely
Bleeding after walking means the artery dissolved
Dressings stop bleeding even while walking
items.exp:
**Answer: A - Walk only when the protocol time has elapsed with a dry groin.** Fresh seals tear under hip flexion and load, so first walking waits for the set hours with a dry wound.
**Why the others are wrong**
- B: Early walking tests nothing but luck
- C: Arteries persist and re-bleed when stressed
- D: Dressings cover rather than stop bleeding
**Key point:** First walking waits for protocol time with dry groins.
items.kp: First ambulation waits for protocol time with a dry groin.
